extracted.intended_audience: social psychologists, researchers and scholars interested in replication, research integrity, and experimental methods in psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and norms for assessing the credibility, replicability, and methodological soundness of experimental research in social psychology, with guidance on common failures (fraud, QRPs, bias) and remedial practices (pre-registration, transparency, replication etiquette).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to fundamental rules of proper scientific research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research must avoid 'violations of fundamental rules of proper scientific research' and not exhibit 'careless, selective and uncritical handling of research and data' as identified by inquiry committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees reviewing Stapel's work concluded that observed flaws were not minor imperfections but violations of fundamental rules; evaluate manuscripts for clear, principled research conduct rather than pervasive sloppiness or selective handling of data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of statistical anomalies / use of statistical review
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical anomalies should be identifiable and flagged by statisticians; statistical review is an essential part of vetting research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many anomalies in Stapel's papers 'were identified readily by statisticians who assisted in the review'; involve independent statistical experts during peer review or post-publication scrutiny to detect improbable patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of outright fraud and grey-area data massaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and prevent both clear fraud and more subtle 'massaging' of data; both undermine credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes a 'sharp line between outright fraud and the “massaging” of data' and that grey-area practices are common; peer reviewers and editors should watch for both fabricated data and questionable data handling practices that artificially enhance results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of questionable research practices (QRPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage in practices identified as QRPs: falsifying data, selectively reporting results, failing to report dependent variables, continuing data collection until significance, presenting unexpected findings as hypothesized, or excluding data to enhance significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on John, Lowenstein, and Prelec's survey: e.g., 1 in 10 admitted falsifying data; 67% selectively reported; 74% failed to report all DVs; 71% continued sampling until significance; 58% excluded data. Peer review should screen for these behaviors and require full disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specification of hypotheses, sample size, and analysis (pre-registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should pre-register hypotheses, projected sample size and composition, and the planned approach to statistical analysis a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include pre-registration at centers such as the Center for Open Science; pre-registration reduces flexibility that leads to false positives and improves transparency about planned analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of negative findings / address publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and researchers should publish negative findings to counteract publication bias and the 'file drawer' problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication bias means journals typically do not publish negative results; encourage venues (e.g., PsychFileDrawer.org) and journal policies that accept null or negative studies; meta-analyses should seek unpublished negative studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of verification bias / acceptance of null hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and reviewers must resist 'verification bias' — a stubborn resistance to accepting the null hypothesis — and avoid practices that repress negative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification bias examples include repeating experiments until they 'work' or excluding inconvenient cases; studies should be designed and reported so null findings are credible and not suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid HARKing (hypothesizing after results are known)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reconstruct or present post hoc findings as if they were a priori hypotheses (HARKing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HARKing misrepresents the objective of the work and treats random events as bona fide achievements; require authors to distinguish exploratory from confirmatory analyses and to disclose post hoc hypothesis generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit researchers' degrees of freedom / disclose analytic flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'researchers’ degrees of freedom' — unjustifiable flexibility in data analysis (multiple DV measures, post-hoc controls, variable selection) that is undisclosed to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreported analytic flexibility inflates false positives. Require full disclosure of all measures, analytic decisions, alternative specifications, and sensitivity analyses to assess robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid p-hacking and cherry-picking results
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage in p-hacking or cherry-picking results to push findings just across the conventional .05 threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links p-hacking and cherry-picking to inflated minimum statistical acceptability; reviewers should request correction for multiple comparisons, report exact p-values, and examine robustness beyond threshold chasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify stopping rules and avoid data-dependent stopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not continue to collect data until a significant result is achieved without proper sequential analysis plans; stopping rules should be pre-specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing to collect data until significance is reached is an example of verification bias; predefine sample sizes or use proper interim analysis methods with appropriate corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint summary tables and make data/methods transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers are advised to preprint their summary tables and make data/methods transparent prior to journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprinting summary tables on personal sites and sharing data increases transparency and allows earlier scrutiny; combine with pre-registration and full methods disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreed replication protocols and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and follow agreed protocols for how replications should be undertaken and evaluated; consider 'etiquette' of involving original authors and transparent correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is 'no agreed protocol' currently; Kahneman suggested proposed replications be outlined to original authors who could assess fairness, and that correspondence be on the record — this reduces acrimony and improves fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose methods appropriate to the phenomena (suitability of experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether experiments are the optimal method for the social phenomena under study; some social regularities may not have recurrent law-like properties amenable to experimental isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues many regularities (norm formation, institutions, mass violence) may not be best studied by laboratory experiments; evaluate methodological fit and consider observational, archival, or qualitative approaches when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of standardization for human-subject experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that experiments on human subjects are difficult to standardize, which can undermine replicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archival inquiries into Milgram, Sherif, Zimbardo show standardization challenges; reviewers should judge whether purported effects are robust to inevitable human-subject variability and whether methods are documented sufficiently to permit replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explicit hypotheses, control groups, and tests of significance in confirmatory work
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory experimental work should state explicit hypotheses, include appropriate control groups, and conduct proper significance testing, rather than presenting demonstrations without these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical social psychology sometimes used demonstrations 'without explicit hypotheses, control groups or tests of significance'; modern confirmatory research should include these elements to be scientifically credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent reporting of all measures and dependent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Report all actual dependent variables and measures used in the study, not just those that yielded significant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The John et al. survey found 74% failed to report all DVs; require full reporting so readers and meta-analysts can assess the extent of selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify exclusion criteria and avoid post-hoc exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and report exclusion criteria (e.g., outlier rules, non-responders) in advance and avoid excluding data post hoc to manufacture significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives the example of excluding cases because individuals didn't respond or were outliers to reduce variance; such exclusions should be justified, pre-specified, and sensitivity-checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent large-scale replication initiatives and collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Support and participate in coordinated replication efforts (e.g., Center for Open Science projects) that attempt to replicate contemporary research using multiple labs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Center for Open Science has initiated unprecedented replication attempts; such collaborative projects increase transparency and provide stronger evidence about robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster a culture of skepticism and rigorous peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate scepticism among reviewers, editors and institutions to prevent an environment of uncritical acceptance that allows dubious practices to persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees found a culture that contributed to absence of skepticism; improving peer review culture (including statistical scrutiny) is necessary to detect dubious findings early.
